932.title: Knowledge as worship
932.hook: whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy a path to the garden (Muslim)
932.howItsDone: Muslims may begin study by setting an intention for God, and study circles meet in mosques and homes to read and discuss the Qur'an and hadith together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great imams' age: Ja'far al-Sadiq, Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, teacher to student to teacher. Your line was: the age of the imams. Did you thank someone who taught you? Day nine hundred thirty-two.

Dark streets before dawn. A student with a borrowed book under one arm, walking across the city to sit in a teacher's circle. The walk is long, and nobody will remember it. Except, says a hadith, it counts. Muslim records the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying that whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him, by it, a path to the garden. Not only the lesson. The path to the lesson. The walk itself is pointed somewhere. Today, the last day of our time with the Abbasids and the House of Wisdom: knowledge as worship.
screen: `A STUDENT WALKING BEFORE DAWN.` → `THE WALK ITSELF COUNTS.` → `A PATH TO THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an keeps knowledge close to prayer. It gives a short plea to say, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." It asks a question that hangs in the air: "Are those who know equal with those who know not?" And the same hadith in Muslim goes on: when people gather in a house of God, reciting the Book and studying it together, tranquility comes down on them and mercy covers them. Study, in a mosque, as a kind of prayer. Which knowledge? Here scholars read differently. Some say the hadith means first of all knowledge of the religion: the Qur'an, the Sunnah, how to pray and live rightly. Others widen it to any useful knowledge sought with a good intention, the healing that helps the sick, the arithmetic that divides an inheritance fairly. Both readings agree on this much: the seeking itself can be devotion. Now look back over the road we've walked since the House of Wisdom. Al-Khwarizmi restoring and balancing. Zero arriving from India. Hospitals that cared for all who came. Al-Biruni measuring the earth, Ibn al-Haytham testing what he thought he knew. Astronomers working out the hours of prayer. Al-Jahiz staring at ants, copyists on the booksellers' street, al-Bukhari sifting reports, the imams teaching in their circles. Different people, different fields, and for some of them the same conviction underneath: learning is something you can offer. Tomorrow we cross the sea to a new land. A path to the garden.
screen: `MY LORD! INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.` · `STUDYING TOGETHER, MERCY COVERS THEM.` · `WHICH KNOWLEDGE? TWO READINGS.` · `LOOKING BACK OVER THE HOUSE OF WISDOM.` · then, large: `A PATH TO THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one thing for Allah, or for the good it can do. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself one honest question: what's one small thing I'd like to understand better? A verse, a word, how something works, a skill someone close to you needs from you. Pick just one. Then think about the why, the way al-Bukhari's book begins with intention. Why do you want to know it? If you pray, you can offer this small bit of learning to God before you start, with the Qur'an's own words: my Lord, increase me in knowledge. If you don't, let the intention be the good it might do. The bell holds the time.
Knowledge as worship. The hadith in Muslim: whoever takes a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to the garden. Today's word.
Your line: a path to the garden. Today, take one actual step toward the thing you chose to learn: open the book, ask the question, watch the lesson. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

933.title: Tariq's mountain
933.hook: Gibraltar is named Jabal Tariq for the commander who crossed the strait
933.howItsDone: Muslim histories remember al-Andalus as a land of faith and learning, and they tell its story beginning with Tariq ibn Ziyad's crossing of the strait.

segments.voice: Yesterday, knowledge as worship, and a look back over the age of the House of Wisdom. Your line was: a path to the garden. Did you take one step toward what you chose to learn? Day nine hundred thirty-three.

A huge limestone rock stands near the southern tip of Spain, staring across a narrow strait at the mountains of Africa. Ships slide past it all day. English speakers call it Gibraltar. Say that slowly, and then say this: Jabal Tariq. By the usual account, that's where the name comes from. Jabal is mountain. Tariq is a man. So every time someone says Gibraltar, they're saying, in a worn-down way, the name of a commander who once crossed that water with an army. We leave Baghdad and go west, to al-Andalus.
screen: `A ROCK FACING AFRICA.` → `GIBRALTAR, JABAL TARIQ.` → `WEST TO AL-ANDALUS.`

segments.voice: Tariq ibn Ziyad served Musa ibn Nusayr, who governed for the Umayyads in North Africa. Tradition remembers Tariq as a Berber, one of the peoples of North Africa, which matters: the story of al-Andalus begins with North Africans as much as Arabs. He crossed the strait with an army, landed by the rock, and marched inland. The Visigothic king, Roderic, met him in battle and was defeated, and the kingdom of the Visigoths came apart. That's how Muslim rule began in the land Arabic writers called al-Andalus, much of what is now Spain and Portugal. For the Christians of the Visigothic kingdom, it was a defeat and the loss of a kingdom; for Muslims, it was the start of a long chapter of life, learning and building in that land. Both memories are real, and both are kept. Then come the legends. Later histories give Tariq a famous speech to his frightened soldiers: the sea is behind you, the enemy before you. Some tellings add that he burned his ships so no one could turn back. These scenes come from later histories, and some historians treat them as legend: stories people tell, the kind that grow around a crossing that changed the map. So hold onto what lasts: a man's name, carried in the name of a rock, said every day by people who've never heard of him. The mountain of Tariq.
screen: `TARIQ, A BERBER COMMANDER.` · `ACROSS THE STRAIT, RODERIC FALLS.` · `A DEFEAT, AND A BEGINNING.` · `THE SEA BEHIND YOU: A LATER LEGEND.` · then, large: `THE MOUNTAIN OF TARIQ.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at a map of the strait, in your mind for now. Settle, and breathe. Picture two continents almost touching. Africa to the south, its mountains rising from the water. Europe to the north, with one great rock standing up at its tip. Between them, a narrow channel of sea. Picture the boats crossing, loaded with people, horses and fear. Then picture the same water today, ferries, fishing boats, and people still crossing it for every reason people cross water. After the bell, if you like, find the strait on a real map. If you pray, you can remember everyone who has crossed it. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Tariq's mountain. Jabal Tariq, the rock named, by the usual account, for Tariq ibn Ziyad, who crossed the strait into al-Andalus. Today's word.
Your line: the mountain of tariq. Today, notice one place name around you and wonder whose name, or which old language, might be hiding inside it. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

934.title: Cordoba, city of lights
934.hook: a great city with lit streets, baths and libraries
934.howItsDone: Cordoba is remembered in Muslim histories as a center of Islamic learning in al-Andalus, and visitors today walk its old streets and its great mosque.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tariq's mountain: a rock that still carries a commander's name, and a crossing into al-Andalus. Your line was: the mountain of tariq. Did you find a name hiding inside a place? Day nine hundred thirty-four.

In a convent in Saxony, far to the north, a nun named Hrotsvitha sits down to write a poem. She is a Christian, writing in Latin, about a Christian boy named Pelagius who died in a Muslim city. And when she names that city, she praises it. She calls it the ornament of the world. A city far from her convent, ruled by people of another faith, and that is what she calls it. The city is Cordoba, on the river Guadalquivir, in the heart of al-Andalus.
screen: `A NUN IN SAXONY WRITES.` → `A CITY RULED BY ANOTHER FAITH.` → `THE ORNAMENT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: What made a faraway nun reach for that phrase? Later Arabic writers, whose accounts al-Maqqari gathered in his history of al-Andalus, describe a city of markets and gardens, public baths, water brought in for drinking and washing, libraries, and streets where you could walk at night by the light of lamps. That's the picture behind the name city of lights. Be a little careful with it. Some of those descriptions were written long after, by people who missed Cordoba, and longing polishes a memory. But the outline holds: this was a capital of books, scholars and craftsmen. And it was a city of more than one faith. Muslims, Christians and Jews lived in its streets, not always in peace, and not always as equals, but close enough to share a language. A Christian writer of Cordoba named Paul Alvarus complained that the young men of his church were so taken with Arabic poetry and Arabic books that they neglected their own Latin. His complaint shows how strong the pull of Arabic culture was, even on those who worried about it. Hrotsvitha's poem holds both sides too. It praises the city, and it is harsh about the ruler at whose order the boy was killed. A golden city, and a real one, with light and shadow. So when you hear the ornament of the world, hear it in a Christian nun's voice, from far away, giving a city of another faith that word. The ornament of the world.
screen: `MARKETS, BATHS, LAMPS, LIBRARIES.` · `LONGING POLISHES A MEMORY.` · `MUSLIMS, CHRISTIANS AND JEWS.` · `LIGHT AND SHADOW, BOTH REAL.` · then, large: `THE ORNAMENT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: The practice: picture a city at night. Settle, and breathe. See a river, dark and slow, and a bridge over it. Beyond, streets with lamps along them, small pools of light. A bath house with steam in the doorway. Someone closing a bookshop. A call to prayer from one direction, a church bell from another, a family lighting candles in a third house. Walk slowly through it in your mind. Notice who is out, who is home, who is still working. Then let the old city fade and see your own street at night, with its own lights and its own people. If you pray, you can hold them all. The bell holds the time.
Cordoba. The capital of al-Andalus on the Guadalquivir, a city of lamps, baths and books that a Saxon nun called the ornament of the world. Today's word.

935.title: The Mosque of Cordoba
935.howItsDone: In a mosque, a mihrab in the qiblah wall shows the direction of prayer toward Mecca, and the rows of worshippers stand facing it; the building in Cordoba is today a Catholic cathedral that visitors may tour.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cordoba: lamps, baths and books, and a Saxon nun's praise. Your line was: the ornament of the world. What generous, true thing did you say about someone else's place? Day nine hundred thirty-five.

Step out of the hard southern sun, through a doorway, into shade. Your eyes take a moment. Then they find columns. Rows of them, in every direction, slim stone trunks rising to arches. And the arches are striped, red brick and pale stone, red and white, red and white, and above them a second tier of arches, as if the trees had grown branches on their branches. You can't see the end of it. Wherever you stand, the rows open away from you. One word fits: a forest. This is the Mosque of Cordoba.
screen: `OUT OF THE SUN, INTO SHADE.` → `RED AND WHITE, RED AND WHITE.` → `ARCHES ON TOP OF ARCHES.`

segments.voice: It was begun under Abd al-Rahman, an Umayyad prince who had escaped to al-Andalus when his family lost power in the east. Later rulers enlarged it again and again, and they kept to the same pattern each time, so the forest simply grew. Historians say some of its columns were taken from older Roman and Visigothic buildings, so the stone itself has lived more than one life. The double arches, by the usual explanation, were a builder's answer to a problem: the columns were short, and stacking arches lifted the roof high enough to let the hall breathe. Here's the thing to notice. To the eye, the forest seems to go every way at once. No single center, no one view. But the people who prayed there did not wander. Every row stood facing one wall, the qiblah wall. And in that wall is the mihrab, a niche that shows worshippers which way to face, later covered with gold mosaic and carved stone. The Qur'an says the places of worship belong to God alone. So a hall with endless paths had one direction built into it. After Christian rulers took Cordoba, the building became a church, and later a cathedral was built up through the middle of the forest. Today it serves as Cordoba's cathedral, and the arches still stand all around it. Visitors walk among them now. A forest of arches.
screen: `BEGUN BY AN UMAYYAD PRINCE.` · `OLD COLUMNS, ARCHES STACKED HIGH.` · `ENDLESS PATHS, ONE DIRECTION.` · `A MOSQUE, THEN A CATHEDRAL.` · then, large: `A FOREST OF ARCHES.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the arches, first in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture yourself standing among the columns. Let the red and white stripes repeat around you, close, then farther, then farther still. Notice how your eye keeps wandering down the rows, looking for an end. Then, gently, turn to face one way and stay there. Let the forest stay wide while you stay pointed. After the bell, if you like, find a photo of the arches and look at it slowly, without scrolling past. If you pray, you can pray with your face turned one way. If you don't, just let your attention settle in one direction. The bell holds the time.
The Mosque of Cordoba. A great hall of red-and-white double arches, built and enlarged by the Umayyads of al-Andalus, and now a cathedral. Today's word.
Your line: a forest of arches. Today, when your attention scatters in every direction, pick one thing and face it for a full minute. Day nine hundred thirty-five.

936.title: Abd al-Rahman III
936.hook: who declared a caliphate in Cordoba
936.howItsDone: The caliphate of Cordoba is remembered in Muslim histories as part of al-Andalus's story of learning and building, and visitors today can walk the excavated ruins of Madinat al-Zahra near Cordoba.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mosque of Cordoba: red-and-white arches in every direction, and every row facing one wall. Your line was: a forest of arches. What did you face for a full minute? Day nine hundred thirty-six.

A story is told in the later histories of al-Andalus. When a great ruler of Cordoba died, after a long reign of victories, building and wealth, a note was found among his things in his own hand. On it he had counted the days of his life when he had been truly happy, free of worry. There were only a handful. Whether it happened exactly that way, nobody can say for certain. But it's told about this man for a reason: he had everything a ruler could want, and the story says it wasn't enough. His name was Abd al-Rahman III.
screen: `A NOTE FOUND AFTER HIS DEATH.` → `ONLY A HANDFUL OF HAPPY DAYS.` → `A RULER WHO HAD EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: He came to power young, over a land in pieces. Rebels held fortresses in the hills, and cities obeyed when it suited them. He spent years in the saddle bringing them back under Cordoba's rule. Then he did something bold. Rulers of al-Andalus before him had called themselves emir, prince. He took the title caliph, and commander of the faithful. Why? In Baghdad, the Abbasid caliph had grown weak. In North Africa, the Fatimids had declared a caliphate of their own, led by Isma'ili Shia imams. Abd al-Rahman answered by claiming the title for Cordoba. Now there was a caliph in the east, a caliph in North Africa, and a caliph in the far west, all at once. For Sunni Muslims, a caliph is the successor who leads the community; Shia Muslims hold that rightful leadership belongs to the Imams of the Prophet's family. The title meant different things depending on who was asking. Under him Cordoba flourished. He built a palace city outside it, Madinat al-Zahra, with halls of marble and gardens. Envoys came from distant kings. A Jewish physician, Hasdai ibn Shaprut, served at his court. But a golden age has a bill. Armies, taxes, campaigns against neighbors, enslaved servants and soldiers in the palace. Later, under his descendants, the caliphate broke apart in civil war, and the palace city was looted and left in ruins. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory." A western caliphate.
screen: `FROM EMIR TO CALIPH.` · `THREE CALIPHS AT ONCE.` · `MADINAT AL-ZAHRA RISES.` · `A GOLDEN AGE HAS A BILL.` · then, large: `A WESTERN CALIPHATE.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about a golden age's cost. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a time that people call golden: in history, in a company, in a family, maybe in your own life. Remember what was good about it, really good. Then ask, gently: who paid for it? Whose work, whose taxes, whose quiet suffering held it up, and who doesn't appear in the story? You don't have to decide it wasn't golden. Just hold the light and the bill side by side. If you pray, you can remember the ones who paid. If you don't, just keep them in view for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Abd al-Rahman III. The ruler of Cordoba who took the title caliph, built Madinat al-Zahra, and, the story says, counted only a handful of happy days. Today's word.
Your line: a western caliphate. Today, when something shines, a product, a party, a plan, ask once who is paying for it. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

937.title: Abbas ibn Firnas
937.hook: a craftsman of Cordoba who, the reports say, strapped on wings and jumped
937.howItsDone: Abbas ibn Firnas is remembered as an inventor of al-Andalus, and his attempted flight is known mainly through the account passed on by the historian al-Maqqari.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abd al-Rahman the Third, the ruler in Cordoba who took the title of caliph. Your line was: a western caliphate. Did you stop to think about what a golden age costs, and who pays it? Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

A man stands on a high place near Cordoba. Feathers are fastened over his body, and a pair of wings is tied to his arms. People have come out to watch. He leans forward, and he jumps. That is how a later historian of al-Andalus, al-Maqqari, tells it, passing on what earlier writers said they saw. The man glides for a stretch, the report says, the way a bird does. Then he comes down hard, and hurts his back. His name was Abbas ibn Firnas, and today belongs to him.
screen: `FEATHERS AND A PAIR OF WINGS.` → `HE JUMPS.` → `HE COMES DOWN HARD.`

segments.voice: Who was he? In the reports, a man of the Cordoba court with many crafts at once: poetry, music, the stars, the making of instruments. The same writers credit him with work on glass made from stone, and with a model of the sky built in his own house. Take those as the reports give them, admiring and a little larger than life. Now the birds. The Qur'an keeps sending its listeners outside to look. In Pickthall's translation: "Have they not seen the birds above them spreading out their wings and closing them?" The verse goes on to say that nothing holds them up except the Beneficent. So looking up at a bird, in this tradition, is already a kind of reading. Abbas looked, and then he tried. Here is the detail worth carrying home. Why did he land so badly? The report has an answer, and it's oddly specific. He had forgotten that birds come down on their tails, so he never made himself one. He studied the wing and missed the tail. A very human mistake: you copy the part you admire and skip the part that looks boring. One honest caution. This is a story told long after, by a writer gathering older accounts. Some readers take it nearly as written; others wonder how much grew in the telling. Nobody can stand on that hill and check. What the story keeps, either way, is a man who wondered about birds, built something, jumped, got hurt, and left behind a lesson about tails. The fall is the part of his story that gets retold. He tried to fly.
screen: `A MAN OF MANY CRAFTS.` · `HAVE THEY NOT SEEN THE BIRDS?` · `HE FORGOT THE TAIL.` · `A REPORT, TOLD LONG AFTER.` · then, large: `HE TRIED TO FLY.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to attempt something new. Settle, and breathe. Let one small thing come to mind that you've never tried. A dish, a stretch, a phrase in another language, a route home, a question you've never asked someone. Keep it small enough to do today. Now picture the first step, only the first one. Then ask the Abbas question: what's my tail? What dull part am I likely to skip? Muslims often say bismillah, in the name of God, before beginning something. If you pray, you can begin your attempt with it. If you don't, just hold the first step in mind. The bell holds the time.
Abbas ibn Firnas. A craftsman of Cordoba who, by the reports, put on wings, jumped, glided, and landed hard for want of a tail. Today's word.
Your line: he tried to fly. Today, try one new thing small enough to finish before bed, and afterward name one thing you'd change next time. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

938.title: Ziryab the musician
938.hook: a musician from Baghdad who brought new music, food and fashion to Cordoba
938.howItsDone: Ziryab is remembered in histories of al-Andalus as a court musician and a setter of taste; Muslim scholars hold a range of views on music and instruments, from permitting them to forbidding them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abbas ibn Firnas, who tied on wings, jumped, and landed hard for want of a tail. Your line was: he tried to fly. What new thing did you try, and what would you change next time? Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

Soup first. Then the meat. Then something sweet to finish. A meal in courses, in a set order, on a table that might have glass on it instead of gold. In the stories of al-Andalus, that order at dinner is credited to one man, and he wasn't a cook. He was a singer from Baghdad with an oud on his back. People called him Ziryab. He came west to Cordoba, and the reports say the city started eating, dressing and even cutting its hair the way he did. Today: Ziryab the musician.
screen: `SOUP, MEAT, THEN SWEETS.` → `A SINGER FROM BAGHDAD.` → `CORDOBA FOLLOWS HIS LEAD.`

segments.voice: The story comes to us mostly through the historian al-Maqqari, gathering older accounts. In Baghdad, it says, Ziryab studied music under a famous master, Ishaq al-Mawsili. The student became too good. When he sang before the caliph, his teacher grew jealous and told him, in effect, to leave or face trouble. So Ziryab went west, and in Cordoba the emir Abd al-Rahman the Second welcomed him into his court. Then come the reports, a long list of them. He added a string to the oud. He played with a plectrum made from an eagle's quill instead of wood. He opened a school of music. And off the stage: meals served in courses, glass vessels on the table, clothes changed with the seasons, a new way to wear the hair. Historians read that list carefully. Some of it may be praise piled on a famous name. But the picture of a court learning taste from one gifted person holds together. So why does a Muslim path spend a day on a singer? Partly because Muslim scholars differ over music, and that's worth saying plainly: some permit instruments, some don't, and others draw lines in between. And partly for a hadith. Sahih Muslim records that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, warned against pride, and a man asked: what if someone likes his clothes to be fine and his sandals good? The answer, in substance: God is beautiful and loves beauty; pride is rejecting the truth and looking down on people. Care for how things look and taste was never the problem in that answer. Contempt was. That fits the week we've walked: knowledge as worship, Tariq's mountain, Cordoba and its mosque, a caliph, a man with wings, and now a man with manners. Music and manners.
screen: `A JEALOUS TEACHER IN BAGHDAD.` · `A NEW LIFE AT CORDOBA'S COURT.` · `A STRING, A QUILL, A MEAL IN COURSES.` · `GOD IS BEAUTIFUL AND LOVES BEAUTY.` · then, large: `MUSIC AND MANNERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to share a new recipe. Settle, and breathe. Think of one dish you love that someone close to you has never had. Maybe a grandmother's, maybe a street food, maybe something you made once and got right. Picture it in order: what goes in first, what it smells like, what it looks like on the plate. Now think of one person to share it with, by cooking it or just by sending the recipe. If you pray, you can give thanks for the food in the words you already know. If you don't, simply notice the gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Ziryab the musician. The singer from Baghdad who, by the reports, taught Cordoba new music, new meals and new manners. Today's word.
Your line: music and manners. Today, share one recipe with someone, and set one meal out with a little care, even if it's just a clean plate and a quiet minute. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.
